Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The issue report describes a problem with TAR file checksum verification failing when the checksum is right aligned and padded with zeros on the left instead of being padded with spaces (NULL-SPACE terminator) on the right as expected by the TAR format.

Examining the method TarUtils.verifyCheckSum(byte[] header) shows that the logic to calculate the stored checksum only processes the first 6 octal digits in the checksum field (CHKSUM_OFFSET to CHKSUM_OFFSET + 6). It specifically looks for characters '0' to '7' and accumulates the value. It stops after 6 digits even though the checksum field length (CHKSUMLEN) is 8 bytes. 

After this processing, it replaces the checksum field bytes with spaces ' ' for the sum calculation, then computes an unsignedSum and signedSum of the entire header with the checksum field replaced by spaces.

Finally, the verification returns true if the parsed storedSum matches either unsignedSum or signedSum.

The problem arises when a TAR archive has its checksum right aligned in the field with zero (0) padding on the left instead of space padding on the right. This causes the last digits of the checksum to be effectively lost or misinterpreted by the current implementation because it strictly only accumulates up to 6 octal digits from the left and ignores any possible other characters, assuming the byte offset after these digits is the start of padding.

In the reading of the headers (TarArchiveInputStream.getNextTarEntry), an instance of TarArchiveEntry is constructed using the byte header. TarArchiveEntry.parseTarHeader calls TarUtils.verifyCheckSum(header) to set the checkSumOK flag. The failure of this checksum verification leads to failure handling or rejecting the archive stream in the test scenario.

The current implementation of verifyCheckSum is rigid in how it processes the checksum field and does not accommodate TAR files that store the checksum right aligned (with leading zero padding). Thus valid TAR archives with this checksum format will be misidentified as invalid.

The issue report's question: "is it necessary to only look at the first 6 octal digits inst" implies that the 6 digit limit is a root cause.

In summary, the bug is due to the verifyCheckSum method's strict scanning only up to 6 octal digits from the beginning of the checksum field, which does not handle right-aligned or differently padded checksum fields, causing valid checksums to fail verification.

No other recent bug reports directly relate to checksum verification or TAR checksum padding issues, so they are not relevant here.

The test testCOMPRESS335 fails because the TAR archive "COMPRESS-335.tar" contains checksum bytes right aligned with zero left padding that is improperly decoded by verifyCheckSum.

---

Methods relevant to fix:
- TarUtils.verifyCheckSum(byte[])
- TarArchiveEntry.parseTarHeader(byte[], ZipEncoding, boolean)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
